c.tagline: The Philippines' historic second city, gateway to island-hopping, diving, and Spanish colonial roots.

taxi.fareNote: White city taxis and yellow airport taxis are metered - insist on the meter, as some drivers push flat rates. Grab and the Angkas motorcycle-taxi app are usually more reliable and transparent on price.

emergency.note: 911 is the national emergency hotline covering police, fire, and medical.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Petty crime around Colon downtown at night; taxi scams

hood_desc: A modern uptown district built around Cebu IT Park's tech towers, with buzzing food parks, rooftop bars, cafes, and nightlife; popular with young professionals and digital nomads.
The city's polished central business district, anchored by the Ayala Center mall, corporate towers, and upscale hotels; a convenient, walkable base for dining and shopping.
The historic core around Magellan's Cross, the Basilica del Santo Niño, and Fort San Pedro - chaotic, crowded, and packed with Spanish-colonial landmarks and street markets; best explored by day.
The neighboring island across the bridges, home to the international airport and a string of beach resorts, dive shops, and island-hopping jump-offs; the go-to for sand and water sports.
A leafy uptown area around the Cebu Provincial Capitol and the Fuente Osmeña rotunda, with hospitals, universities, and mid-range hotels; central and local in feel.

water.note: Tap water is not reliably potable; stick to bottled or filtered water.

transit.pay: Jeepneys are cash-only, with a few-peso fare passed hand-to-hand to the driver. MyBus and modern jeepneys use a low flat fare paid on board or via a Beep contactless card. Grab and Angkas (motorcycle taxi) are the easy app options.
transit.hours: Jeepneys and buses run roughly from dawn to late evening, thinning out after about 10 PM; Grab and taxis fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Cebu has no rail or metro. Getting around relies on jeepneys - the ubiquitous shared minibuses - plus the newer air-conditioned MyBus and modern-jeepney routes, taxis, and app-based Grab cars and Angkas motorcycle taxis. A long-planned Cebu Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system is still under construction.

food.name: Puso and street barbecue

food.name: Sutukil seafood
food.desc: Buy the fish, then choose sugba (grilled), tuwa (sour soup) or kilaw (raw in vinegar). One catch, three preparations, all at once.

places.name: Lantaw Floating Native Restaurant

places.name: Pasil Fish Market
places.note: Cebu's dawn fish market; buy the catch and have neighbouring stalls cook it.

food.desc: Cebu's signature pasalubong: chewy sweet-tart dried mango strips, plus danggit rabbitfish dried and salted for a crisp breakfast fry-up.

food.name: Ngohiong
food.desc: Cebu's take on the Hokkien spring roll: five-spiced vegetable and pork filling in a beancurd wrapper, deep-fried and dunked in sweet-sour sauce.

places.name: Original Ngohiong sa Colon
places.note: Downtown stalls on the country's oldest street; the ngohiong heartland.

places.name: Carbon Public Market
places.note: Cebu's oldest market, good for ngohiong, balbacua and cheap eats before dark.

places.name: Sugbo Mercado
places.note: Several stalls sell ngohiong in a safer evening setting with seating.

food.name: Humba
food.desc: Cebuano braised pork belly with soy, vinegar, palm sugar, black beans and banana blossom; sweeter and darker than Luzon adobo.

places.name: Golden Cowrie Native Restaurant
places.note: Family-style Filipino restaurant; humba, kinilaw and crispy pata with free dips.

places.name: STK ta Bay!
places.note: Native-style restaurant popular with locals for humba and seafood platters.

places.name: Lantaw Native Restaurant
places.note: Hilltop branch pairing Cebuano home cooking with a city-lights view.

food.name: Tuba
food.desc: Fresh coconut palm sap wine, cloudy and mildly sour, sometimes reddened with tungog bark; drunk from shared cups at grills and markets.

places.name: Lantaw Floating Native Restaurant

places.name: Larsian sa Fuente

food.desc: Cebu carabao mangoes blended with ice and a little milk; the local antidote to the heat and to a lechon-heavy lunch.

landmarks: Magellan's Cross
Housed in an octagonal chapel, this cross commemorates the 1521 arrival of Ferdinand Magellan and Christianity in the Philippines, making it a top historical photo stop.
Basilica Minore del Santo Niño
The oldest Roman Catholic church in the Philippines draws millions of pilgrims to venerate its centuries-old image of the Child Jesus.
Fort San Pedro
The oldest and smallest triangular Spanish fort in the country, with thick coral-stone walls overlooking the harbor, is a beautifully preserved piece of colonial history.
Cebu Taoist Temple
Perched in the hills of Beverly Hills subdivision, this colorful Chinese temple with dragon-adorned gates offers panoramic city views and striking architecture.
Temple of Leah
Dubbed the 'Taj Mahal of Cebu,' this grand Roman-style monument built as a tribute to a late wife is one of the city's most Instagrammed modern landmarks.
Sirao Flower Garden
Known as Cebu's 'Little Amsterdam,' this hillside garden bursts with celosia flowers in rainbow colors, a favorite for vibrant photo backdrops.
Tops Lookout
Set high above the city, this viewpoint delivers a spectacular panorama of Cebu City, Mactan Island, and the sea, especially magical at sunset.
Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral
This stately 19th-century cathedral with a distinctive octagonal dome anchors Cebu's historic downtown and remains the seat of the Archdiocese of Cebu.
Casa Gorordo Museum
A beautifully restored 19th-century ancestral house showcases Cebuano heritage and colonial-era domestic life in the historic Parian district.
Yap-Sandiego Ancestral House
One of the oldest residential structures in the Philippines, this coral-stone and hardwood house offers a rare glimpse into 17th-century Cebuano living.

train.note: There is no railway on Cebu or anywhere in the Visayas - the Philippines' only passenger rail is around Manila, and even that is largely suspended. Travel here is by road, ferry or plane, and Mactan-Cebu airport is the country's second international gateway.

bus.note: No international coaches. Cebu South Bus Terminal serves Moalboal, Oslob and the southern towns, and the North Bus Terminal covers Bantayan and Malapascua; Ceres Liner is the dominant operator and some services roll straight onto ferries to Negros and Leyte. Buy at the terminal - online booking is limited. MyBus links the terminals with the SM malls.

ferry.note: No international sailings, but Cebu is the busiest ferry hub in the Philippines and the boats are proper transport, not excursions. OceanJet's fast craft from Pier 1 reach Bohol in about two hours with several departures a day; 2GO's larger overnight ships run the long routes from Pier 4. Sailings are suspended when a typhoon signal is raised between roughly June and November, so build in slack around flights.

full.name: Bohol (Chocolate Hills & Tarsiers)

full.name: Moalboal & Pescador Island
full.blurb: The famous sardine run and turtle-filled reefs on the southwest coast, a couple of hours from the city.
